newsitem.title: UK: British government calls for public sector pay freeze.
newsitem.headline: British government calls for public sector pay freeze.

text.p: British public sector pay should effectively be frozen in 1997, with most employees receiving wage increases below the rate of inflation, the government said on Tuesday.
The announcement came just hours after four teaching unions called for pay rises above inflation.

"The government remains determined to contain public spending and suggests that pay recommendations for 1997 should be set at lower levels than this year to reflect the changed economic context," Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke said.

"With inflation low, and expected to continue to fall, public sector settlements must adjust to reflect this, and to be affordable within budgets," he said in his annual submission to the public-sector Pay Review Bodies.
The British government does not set pay limits centrally but insists that wage increases should be offset by increased efficiency.
The teachers' unions said children's education would suffer if the government imposed another pay increase to be funded out of efficiency savings.

"Class sizes have risen again this year, stress on teachers and the demands they face continue to increase. But still the Government refuses to recognise the damage to morale and performance such a situation causes," said Doug McAvoy, general secretary of the National Union of Teachers, the largest union.
"Our teachers deserve better treatment. They have a right to expect that their salaries will reflect the importance of their work."
The squeeze on the public sector contrasts with developments in top-level private-sector pay.
Research group Income Data Services said the highest paid directors at Britain's largest public companies received average pay increases of 12.6 percent this year.
